newsitem.title: CUBA: Spanish firms in Cuba worried by U.S. detention.
newsitem.headline: Spanish firms in Cuba worried by U.S. detention.

text.p: Spanish firms doing business in Cuba said on Wednesday they were concerned about the detention in Miami of a Spanish businessman accused of breaking the U.S. economic embargo against the island.
Javier Ferreiro, a resident of Havana, was detained last week by U.S. Customs for illegally sending U.S. goods worth some $350,000 to Cuba via the Dominican Republic.

Rafael Garcia Aznar, president of the Association of Spanish Business in Cuba (AEEC), said his group had written to Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes expressing concern about the detention and what AEEC saw as a lack of support from the Spanish government on the case.
"They (the Foreign Ministry) should have reacted much more firmly," Garcia said.

Ferreiro, 45, was arrested on April 1 in Key Biscayne, an exclusive island near Miami, on a charge of violating the Trading With The Enemy Act. He faced a possible penalty of 10 years in prison and a $500,000 fine, U.S. authorities said.
A judge on Thursday ordered Ferreiro held without bond.

Garcia contrasted Spain's attitude to Ferreiro's detention with its vigorous response last month in the case of a Spanish tourist, Jesus Martin, prevented from leaving Cuba after being involved in a traffic accident. Matutes threatened to advise Spaniards not to travel to Cuba if the Martin case were not rapidly resolved, prompting a furious reply from Cuba.

Garcia said the AEEC represents some 40 of more than 100 Spanish firms doing business in Cuba, who make up one fifth of all foreign firms on the island. Spain is a leading trade partner of Cuba with bilateral trade worth some $500 annually.

The Cuban Foreign Ministry has not so far commented on the case. But the deputy president of Cuba's Council of Ministers, Jose Ramon Fernandez, told Spanish reporters in Havana on Tuesday that Ferreiro's detention signalled the United States was "trying to terrorise Spanish businessmen so that they don't invest or do business here."

The fact that U.S. products can be bought in Cuba demonstrates the embargo is far from watertight. They are imported into Cuba via third countries in the region, meaning there is probably little way a company seeking to abide by the law can ensure its products are not destined for Cuba.
